projects.title: Realtime Fleet Telemetry Pipeline
projects.summary: Sub-minute vehicle telemetry for an 1,800-van fleet, from Kafka topics through Spark into Snowflake and ops dashboards.
projects.heroSummary: Replacing a nightly batch load with a streaming pipeline that puts vehicle telemetry in front of the operations team in under a minute.
problemStatement: Telemetry from 1,800 vans — GPS, fuel, engine fault codes — landed in the warehouse once a night. Depot managers were making dispatch decisions on data that was up to 26 hours old, and a fault code raised at 9am was invisible until the next morning.
The nightly job also failed loudly and often: a single malformed device payload aborted the whole load, and there was no way to reprocess a subset without rerunning eleven hours of history.

architecture.caption: FIG. 02 — END-TO-END DATA FLOW, DEVICE TO DASHBOARD

pipeline.title: Ingestion
pipeline.description: Devices publish to MQTT; a bridge writes to partitioned Kafka topics with per-device keys and a 7-day retention window.

pipeline.title: Transformation
pipeline.description: Spark Structured Streaming decodes protobuf, validates against the schema registry, and routes bad payloads to a quarantine topic.

pipeline.title: Storage
pipeline.description: Micro-batches land in Snowflake raw tables every 20 seconds; dbt incremental models build the vehicle-hour fact layer.

pipeline.title: Serving
pipeline.description: Depot dashboards read from a materialised serving view; fault codes also fire a webhook into the maintenance queue.

dataModel.summary: The serving layer is a narrow star schema: one fact per grain, dimensions conformed with the finance models so depot cost and vehicle utilisation join without a bridge table.

tables.name: fct_vehicle_reading
tables.description: Validated telemetry at source resolution, clustered on vehicle and reading timestamp. 42M rows a day, 30-day hot window.

tables.name: fct_vehicle_hour
tables.description: Distance, idling minutes, fuel burn and fault counts rolled to the hour. This is the table dashboards actually query.

tables.name: dim_vehicle
tables.description: Registration, depot assignment, model and telematics firmware version, history preserved so old readings keep their context.

tables.name: dim_depot
tables.description: Region, shift pattern and cost centre, shared with the finance mart so utilisation and spend reconcile.

dataModel.footnote: 24 MODELS · 61 TESTS · SOURCES CONTRACT-TESTED ON FRESHNESS AND ROW COUNT

infrastructure.label: Provisioning
infrastructure.description: Terraform modules for MSK, the Spark cluster and Snowflake roles and warehouses. One plan per environment, applied only through CI — no console changes.

infrastructure.label: Runtime
infrastructure.description: The MQTT bridge and streaming jobs run as Docker images on ECS Fargate; managed Airflow triggers the dbt runs and the hourly fuel-card pull.

infrastructure.label: Environments
infrastructure.description: dev → staging → prod, each with its own Snowflake database and topic prefix. Staging replays a 1% sample of live traffic, so schema changes fail there first.

infrastructure.label: Observability
infrastructure.description: Grafana on consumer lag and job duration, dbt artifacts pushed to a freshness board, and an on-call page when the quarantine topic grows faster than it drains.

challenges.challenge: Devices went offline in rural areas and replayed hours of buffered events at once, producing duplicate and out-of-order records.
challenges.solution: Event-time watermarking with a 6-hour tolerance plus a dedupe key on device ID and reading timestamp, enforced in the Spark job and again as a dbt test.

challenges.challenge: Streaming into Snowflake naively meant a warehouse running 24/7 and a credit bill three times the batch pipeline it replaced.
challenges.solution: Micro-batch buffering at 20-second intervals on a small warehouse with auto-suspend, and hot aggregates kept narrow so dashboards never scan raw events.

challenges.challenge: Firmware updates changed payload fields without warning, silently breaking downstream fuel metrics.
challenges.solution: A schema registry with compatibility checks in CI, and a contract test that pages the on-call engineer before the data reaches the fact layer.

results.label: End-to-end data latency, device to dashboard
Pipeline uptime over 12 months in production
Annual fuel saving from idling alerts in year one
Warehouse spend against the batch pipeline it replaced

writeUp.lead: A longer account of the project — why streaming was the right call here, and where it wasn't.
body: The business case was never really about latency. Depot managers had learned to distrust the morning report, so they phoned drivers instead — the pipeline's job was to make a screen more reliable than a phone call. That framing changed what we built: fewer metrics, defined precisely, with freshness printed next to every number.

Most of the engineering effort went into the unglamorous half: the quarantine topic, the replay tooling, and the contract tests that stop a firmware release from quietly changing what "fuel level" means.

retro.title: What I would do differently
retro.text: I would put the hourly aggregate in front of users on day one and hold the raw fact layer back until someone asked for it. We spent six weeks tuning a table that three people ever queried directly.

projects.title: Retail Margin Warehouse Rebuild
projects.summary: 240 tested dbt models replacing a 900-line stored procedure. Month-end close went from four days to one.
projects.heroSummary: Rebuilding a decade-old stored-procedure warehouse as a tested, documented dbt project the finance team could trust.
problemStatement: The margin mart was a single 900-line stored procedure, written over a decade by rotating contractors, that nobody fully understood. It ran once a night, took four days to fully reconcile after any change, and finance kept a shadow spreadsheet because they didn't trust it.
There were no tests, no documentation and no way to tell which upstream table change had broken a downstream number until someone in finance noticed the total looked wrong.

architecture.caption: FIG. 02 — SOURCE SYSTEMS TO MARGIN MART

pipeline.title: Ingestion
pipeline.description: Fivetran connectors land POS, supplier cost and hierarchy data into a raw Snowflake schema, unchanged from source.

pipeline.title: Transformation
pipeline.description: dbt staging models standardise types and naming; intermediate models encode the margin logic previously buried in the stored procedure.

pipeline.title: Storage
pipeline.description: Mart-layer models are incremental, clustered on store and date, with snapshot models preserving historical cost changes.

pipeline.title: Serving
pipeline.description: Looker explores read directly from the mart layer; finance's close checklist runs a dbt test suite before sign-off.

dataModel.summary: A conformed star schema replaces the procedural logic: one fact at the store-SKU-day grain, with margin components broken into their own columns instead of a single opaque total.

tables.name: fct_margin_daily
tables.description: Revenue, cost, markdown and margin components at daily grain, replacing the stored procedure's single output table.

tables.name: dim_product
tables.description: Product hierarchy and supplier cost history, versioned so historical margin recalculates correctly after a hierarchy change.

dataModel.footnote: 240 MODELS · 640 TESTS · FULL LINEAGE DOCUMENTED IN DBT DOCS

infrastructure.label: Provisioning
infrastructure.description: Snowflake roles and warehouses managed as Terraform, one warehouse per workload so finance queries never queue behind the nightly build.

infrastructure.label: Runtime
infrastructure.description: dbt Cloud runs the nightly build and a lighter intraday refresh; Airflow triggers the Fivetran syncs it depends on.

infrastructure.label: Environments
infrastructure.description: A dedicated CI database rebuilds the full project on every pull request against a sampled dataset.

infrastructure.label: Observability
infrastructure.description: dbt test results and freshness checks post to a finance-close Slack channel every morning.

challenges.challenge: Finance needed the new mart to match the old procedure's numbers exactly before they would sign off on cutting over.
challenges.solution: A parallel-run period with an automated reconciliation model diffing old vs new output row-by-row, tracked to zero discrepancies before go-live.

challenges.challenge: Migrating logic out of a stored procedure risked silently losing edge-case handling nobody remembered was there.
challenges.solution: Paired sessions with the original finance analyst to extract undocumented business rules before touching the SQL.

results.label: Finance sign-off without a shadow spreadsheet

writeUp.lead: Why rewriting a decade-old stored procedure was less about SQL and more about winning back trust.
body: The hardest part wasn't the transformation logic — it was convincing finance that a system they'd learned to route around by hand was worth trusting again. Documentation and tests did more for adoption than any performance improvement.

retro.title: What I would do differently
retro.text: I'd have started the parallel-run reconciliation in week one instead of week six — it became the thing that actually built confidence, and it should have shaped the whole project timeline.

projects.title: Supplier Ingestion Framework
projects.summary: Config-driven ingestion for 60 supplier feeds across SFTP, CSV and API, with schema-drift alerting built in.
projects.heroSummary: One configurable framework replacing 60 bespoke, hand-maintained supplier ingestion scripts.
problemStatement: Each of the 60 supplier feeds — a mix of SFTP drops, CSV exports and a handful of REST APIs — had its own bespoke script, written by whoever onboarded that supplier. Half were undocumented, and a format change from a supplier could break a script for weeks before anyone noticed.
Onboarding a new supplier took two to three days of engineering time, most of it copy-pasting and adjusting an existing script rather than writing anything new.

dataSources.format: Ad hoc, via a lightweight upload form

pipeline.title: Ingestion
pipeline.description: A per-supplier YAML config declares connection details and expected schema; a single Airflow DAG factory generates one DAG per supplier from it.

pipeline.title: Transformation
pipeline.description: Incoming files are validated against the declared schema; drift beyond a configured tolerance quarantines the file and pages the data team.

pipeline.title: Storage
pipeline.description: Validated files land in a raw S3 zone, then load into Postgres staging tables, partitioned by supplier and date.

pipeline.title: Serving
pipeline.description: Downstream dbt models pick up from the staging tables; a supplier health dashboard shows freshness and error counts per feed.

infrastructure.label: Provisioning
infrastructure.description: Each supplier's config is a YAML file in version control; a merged PR is the entire onboarding process.

infrastructure.label: Runtime
infrastructure.description: The ingestion workers run as a Docker image on Airflow's KubernetesExecutor, scaling per feed volume.

infrastructure.label: Environments
infrastructure.description: A staging Airflow instance replays historical files nightly to catch config regressions before production.

infrastructure.label: Observability
infrastructure.description: Per-supplier freshness and row-count checks feed a dashboard, with alerting on missed drops or schema drift.

challenges.challenge: Suppliers changed file formats without notice, and the old scripts failed silently or produced corrupt loads.
challenges.solution: Schema validation on every file against a declared contract, with drift routed to a quarantine bucket and a Slack alert instead of a bad load.

challenges.challenge: Sixty different bespoke scripts meant sixty different ways for the same class of bug to reappear.
challenges.solution: Collapsing all suppliers onto one framework and a shared test suite, so a fix or improvement applies to every feed at once.

results.label: Supplier feeds on one shared framework
Time to onboard a new supplier
Silent bad loads since schema validation shipped

writeUp.lead: Turning 60 one-off scripts into a single configurable framework, and what made suppliers' trust in the data go up rather than down.
body: The framework itself was straightforward engineering. The harder problem was organisational: getting each supplier relationship owner to agree on what a valid file actually looked like, often for the first time.

retro.title: What I would do differently
retro.text: I'd have built the quarantine-and-alert path before the framework itself, rather than after — it would have surfaced how messy some suppliers' data really was much earlier.

projects.title: Self-Serve Metrics Platform
projects.summary: A metrics layer and Looker environment provisioned by Terraform, with query-cost caps and usage tracking.
projects.heroSummary: Giving every team a governed, self-serve way to define and query metrics without a data-team ticket queue.
problemStatement: Every team wanted their own metric defined slightly differently, and every request went through the same two-person data team. The backlog was three weeks deep, and two teams had started keeping their own spreadsheet definitions that quietly disagreed with each other.
There was also no visibility into who was running what query, so a handful of unoptimised dashboards were responsible for most of the warehouse spend.

architecture.caption: FIG. 02 — METRICS LAYER AND SELF-SERVE ENVIRONMENT

pipeline.title: Ingestion
pipeline.description: Teams define metrics as YAML against existing BigQuery marts — no new pipelines, just a shared definition layer on top.

pipeline.title: Transformation
pipeline.description: A metrics compiler validates definitions against a style guide and compiles them into LookML, checked in CI before merge.

pipeline.title: Storage
pipeline.description: Compiled LookML deploys to a dedicated Looker project per domain, each with its own BigQuery reservation and cost cap.

pipeline.title: Serving
pipeline.description: Teams explore their own metrics in Looker directly; a usage dashboard tracks query cost per team against their monthly budget.

infrastructure.label: Provisioning
infrastructure.description: Terraform provisions a Looker project, BigQuery reservation and IAM group per onboarded team, from a single module.

infrastructure.label: Runtime
infrastructure.description: The metrics compiler runs as a scheduled Kubernetes job on merge to main, redeploying changed LookML projects only.

infrastructure.label: Environments
infrastructure.description: A sandbox Looker instance lets teams preview compiled metrics against a cost-capped BigQuery slot before requesting production access.

infrastructure.label: Observability
infrastructure.description: Per-team query cost and slot usage feed a shared dashboard, with a soft-cap warning before a team's monthly budget is spent.

challenges.challenge: Letting every team define their own metrics risked recreating the same inconsistency problem, just self-served instead of centralised.
challenges.solution: A required style guide and CI validation step that checks new metric definitions against existing ones for naming and logic conflicts before merge.

challenges.challenge: Self-serve access to BigQuery risked runaway query costs from inexperienced analysts.
challenges.solution: Per-team BigQuery reservations with hard slot caps, so an expensive query slows down rather than spiking the shared bill.

results.label: Time from metric request to availability
Conflicting metric definitions since the style-guide check shipped

screenshots.caption: FIG. 03 — TEAM USAGE AND COST DASHBOARD

writeUp.lead: Building a self-serve metrics platform that stayed governed instead of turning into twelve teams' worth of new spreadsheet disagreements.
body: The Terraform and Looker plumbing was the easy 20%. Most of the actual work was the style guide and the CI check that enforces it — the part that keeps self-serve from just relocating the original inconsistency problem.

retro.title: What I would do differently
retro.text: I'd have capped BigQuery reservations from day one instead of week four. The first month's bill was a rough surprise that a smaller default cap would have prevented entirely.
